### ex-the-interval-the-cantor-set-and-the-hilbert-cube-are-compact — CERTIFY

ASSESSMENT: Correct and aligned with the proof. `thm-heine-borel-rn` states that a subset of the real line is compact exactly when closed and bounded. `thm-cantor-set-properties` says the Cantor set is “closed and bounded, hence compact,” while `thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact` states “Closed in compact is compact.” Most importantly, `thm-tychonoff` begins “Assume the Axiom of Choice” and concludes that the product of compact spaces is compact. The title now preserves that hypothesis.

Nothing below uses compactness of $S^1$. [L5]" " [L9] A closed bounded interval of $\mathbb{R}$ is compact in the open-cover sense of real analysis ([[thm-heine-borel-r]]); that notion agrees with metric compactness (claim 5 of [[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]]), which in turn agrees with compactness of the subspace in the topological sense (claim 2 of [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]]), so such an interval is a compact subset of the topological space $\mathbb{R}$."

### ex-sigma-compactness-and-lindelof-in-the-line-and-the-rationals — CERTIFY
CURRENT TEXT READ: "Claims 1, 2 and 4 are theorems of ZF. Claim 3 spends countable choice twice: once to name a finite subcover for each of countably many pieces, and once more through [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]], which is what makes the union of those countably many finite families at most countable." "[L4] $\mathbb{Q}$ is countably infinite, so there is a surjection $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Q}$, and every **nonempty** at most countable family may be indexed by $\mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-rationals-countable]], [[def-countable]], [[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]])." "[L10] Assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice, a union $\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n$ of at most countable sets indexed by $\mathbb{N}$ is at most countable ([[thm-countable-union-of-countable]], [[def-countable-choice]])." "For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the set $T_n$ of finite subfamilies of $\mathcal{U}$ covering $I_n$ is nonempty, $I_n$ being compact by step 1.1 and the ambient reading being licensed by [L9], so [L5] supplies $\mathcal{V}_n \in T_n$ for every $n$; the union $\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \mathcal{V}_n$ is an at most countable subfamily of $\mathcal{U}$ by [L10], being a countable union of finite sets, and covers $\mathbb{R}$ by step 1.1."
ASSESSMENT: Correct. `thm-rationals-countable` says the rationals are countably infinite. `lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n` begins “Let A be a nonempty set” and gives the equivalence with being a surjective image of the naturals, so the restored nonemptiness hypothesis is exact. `def-countable-choice` supplies simultaneous choices from the nonempty sets of finite subcovers. `thm-countable-union-of-countable` begins “Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice” and concludes that the indexed union is at most countable. `lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient` supplies the ambient-cover formulation used to make each finite-subcover set nonempty. The rest of the four claims is correct.

### ex-the-sorgenfrey-line-is-lindelof-and-its-square-is-not — REFUSE
CURRENT TEXT READ: `title: "$\\mathbb{R}$ with the half-open intervals $[a,b)$ as a basis is not compact and, assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice, is Lindel\\\"of, while its square is not Lindel\\\"of, the antidiagonal being an uncountable closed discrete subspace"`
ASSESSMENT: The repaired title is honest: `def-countable-choice` supplies the choice used in step 4.1, while the noncompactness and closed-discrete-antidiagonal arguments are otherwise valid. However, the Remark still falsely says: “In the square the antidiagonal is a set on which every basic box is a single point” and “the boxes never contain two of them at once.” Only the specially constructed box at each antidiagonal point has singleton intersection. A basic box such as `[0,10) × [-10,1)` contains uncountably many antidiagonal points. This is a concrete false mathematical claim in a Remark.
COLLATERAL: The title repair itself broke nothing; refusal is for the surviving false Remark.

### cex-a-continuous-image-of-a-locally-compact-space — CERTIFY
CURRENT TEXT READ: "[L3] The canonical-natural map $\iota$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, and satisfies $\iota(n+1) = \iota(n) + 1$ ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]], [[def-canonical-natural]], [[def-natural-numbers]]), so distinct naturals have distinct canonical naturals and the members of $N$ are spaced at distance at least $1$; and for every real $t$ there is a natural $n$ with $t < \iota(n)$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]])."
ASSESSMENT: Correct. `lem-of-naturals-positive` states that the canonical-natural map “is strictly increasing, hence injective” and supplies the addition law. `def-canonical-natural` supplies the recursion by adding one at successors, including the zero case together with positivity. `thm-of-archimedean` says, equivalently, that “the canonical naturals are cofinal.” These facts license the spacing, injectivity and unboundedness used later. The quotient construction and closed infinite discrete obstruction are valid.

### ex-the-alexander-subbase-lemma-applied-to-a-closed-interval — CERTIFY
CURRENT TEXT READ: `title: "Assuming the Axiom of Choice, compactness of $[0,1]$ derived from the subbase lemma alone, using only the rays as a subbasis and the least upper bound property"` "Then, assuming the Axiom of Choice, $L$ is compact ([[def-compact-space]]), and the proof below uses only [[thm-alexander-subbase-lemma]], which is where that hypothesis is spent, and the least upper bound property of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]): no bisection, no metric, and no sequence." "[L1] Alexander's subbase lemma, assuming the Axiom of Choice in the form of Zorn's lemma: if $\mathcal{S}$ is a subbasis for the topology of a space $Z$ and every family $\mathcal{S}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{S}$ with $\bigcup \mathcal{S}_0 = Z$ has a finite subfamily with union $Z$, then $Z$ is compact ([[thm-alexander-subbase-lemma]], [[def-topology-basis-subbasis]])." "The order topology of $L$ and the subspace topology $L$ inherits from the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$ are compared nowhere below; every statement here is about the order topology alone ([[def-subspace-topology-top]], [[def-metrizable-space]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]])."
ASSESSMENT: Correct. `thm-alexander-subbase-lemma` begins “Assume the Axiom of Choice” and states exactly that the finite-subcover property for covers drawn from a fixed subbasis implies compactness. `def-topology-basis-subbasis` defines a subbasis through the topology it generates. The moved scope sentence accurately distinguishes the trace topology defined by `def-subspace-topology-top`, the metric topology defined by `def-metric-topology`, and the usual topology named by `lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space`; none is used in the verification. The supremum argument correctly reduces an arbitrary ray cover to two rays.
